figure_candidates.label: Figure 1
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 1.   Identification of glycosylated cannabinoids in C. sativa flowers. (A) Representation of the cannabinoid biosynthetic pathway illustrating the key enzymes 
involved in cannabinoid production and their cellular location. Known biosynthetic genes are marked in blue, and UDP-­glycosyltransferases (UGTs) identified in 
this study are marked in red. Position of glycosylation in CBGA and CBDA is putative. (B) LC–MS extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) of glycosylated intermediates 
(i.e., OA and DA) and cannabinoids (i.e., CBGA, CBDA, THCA, CBCA, and CBNA) detected in the negative ionization mode [M-­H]-­ in mature female flowers of 
five C. sativa cultivars. Chromatograms were normalized to the highest value. In the absence of chemical standards, glycosylated metabolites synthesized by 
recombinant O. sativa enzyme (OsUGT) were used as reference for identification based on similarity in exact mass, retention time, and fragmentation pattern. 
Glycosylated metabolites which are structural isomers, are labeled #1 #2 or #3 according to their retention times (SI Appendix, Table S2). Potential glycosylation 
sites are highlighted in red on each substrate structure.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 2.   Correlation between olivetolic acid glycosides and cannabinoid accumulation in C. sativa flowers. (A) Selected extracted ion chromatogram (EIC) of Olivetolic 
Acid Glycoside 1 (OAG1) and OAG3 isomers, highlighting their different accumulation pattern in a single high-­THCA plant across tissues and floral developmental 
stages. Product of recombinant O. sativa enzyme (OsUGT) assay with OA as substrate was used as reference. Chromatograms were normalized to the highest 
value. (B) Normalized (relative) and (C) absolute levels of THCA, CBGA, OA, OAG1, and OAG3 in different tissues and flowers at various developmental stages. 
Quantification of OAG1 and OAG3 was performed based on hydrolysis reaction using an external calibration curve (SI Appendix, Fig. S5). Concentrations are 
parts per million (ppm) per fresh weight of tissue; mean ± SD; n = 3 biological replicates. FF; female flowers. Nd: not detected.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 3.   Mining for candidate C. sativa cannabinoid UDP-­glycosyltransferases by phylogenetic and gene expression analysis. (A) Phylogenetic tree of 129 proteins 
annotated as UGTs from C. sativa, alongside selected UGTs from Arabidopsis thaliana and UGTs that have been shown to glycosylate OA and cannabinoids from 
Helichrysum umbraculigerum, Oryza sativa, and Stevia rebaudiana (amino acid sequences are provided in Dataset S1). The maximum-­likelihood tree was constructed 
in MEGAX using 1,000 bootstrap replications. Bootstrap values are indicated at the nodes of each branch. (B) Heatmap of normalized raw reads (mean; n = 3) for 
50 of the most highly expressed C. sativa UGT genes in representative tissues, and five known cannabinoid biosynthetic genes (AAE1, GOT, OLS, OAC, and CBDAS). 
The full dataset is provided in Dataset S2. (C) Quantitative real-­time PCR (qRT-­PCR) analysis of gene expression in a single high-­THCA plant across tissues and 
floral developmental stages (mean; n = 3 biological replicates). Expression levels were normalized to the ACTIN3 gene and calculated as fold change using leaves 
as the reference tissue. Asterisks indicate significant differences between leaves and other tissues, determined by two-­sided Student’s t test (exact *P < 0.05, 
**P < 0.01). FF-­female flowers; 3, 6, 9, and 12 wk from flowering initiation.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 4.   Activity and kinetics of the CsUGT11 and CsUGT14 enzymes. (A) LC–MS extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) showing glycosylated products formed 
in vitro by CsUGT11 and CsUGT14 using UDP-­Glc as the sugar donor. Glycosylated products from S. rebaudiana UGT (SrUGT) served as references. Glycosylated 
metabolites which are structural isomers, are labeled #1 #2 or #3 according to their retention times (SI Appendix, Table S2). Chromatograms were normalized to 
the most abundant product. (B and C) Steady-­state kinetic analysis of CsUGT11 and CsUGT14 with OA as substrate and UDP-­Glc as donor. Absolute concentrations 
of OAG1 and OAG2 were quantified using an OA calibration curve. Kinetic parameters were determined by nonlinear regression model (mean ± s.d., n = 3 
independent assays).

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 5.   Isomer switch following CsUGT14 protein design. (A) Recombinant enzyme assays with 33 FuncLib tool variants (M1-­M33) of the CsUGT14 protein with 
OA as substrate and UDP-­Glc as a sugar donor. Bars represent the ratio of peak areas of OAG1 and OAG2, highlighting the shift in the isomer produced by the 
enzyme. The letters E or Q above indicate the amino acid identity in position 86 of the protein. A full list of mutations introduced in each variant appears in 
SI Appendix, Table S3. Structural models of (B) wild type (WT) CsUGT14 and (C) its M3 variant, each complexed with UDP-­Glc (green sticks) and docked OA (purple 
sticks). In the WT (B), electrostatic repulsion between the carboxyl group of Glu86 (E86) and OA (marked in blue) orients OA for OAG2 isomer formation, whereas 
in the M3 variant (C) with Glu86 mutated to Gln86 (Q86) this repulsion is reduced, repositioning OA to favor OAG1 isomer production.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 6
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 6.   Stabilizing and shifting CsUGT14 enzyme activity toward cannabinoids through protein design. Recombinant enzyme assays were performed using 33 
stabilized CsUGT14 variants (S1–S33) with OA, CBGA, CBDA, CBCA, or THCA as substrates, and UDP-­Glc as the sugar donor. Product amounts were quantified 
using cannabinoid-­specific calibration curves and normalized to protein levels based on SDS-­PAGE analysis. (A) Total glycosylation activity of each variant as 
a sum of all cannabinoids activity versus OA, highlighting 8 variants with more than 10-­fold increased glycosylation of cannabinoids as compared to the WT 
unmodified CsUGT14 enzyme. (B) Glycosylation activity for each substrate across all variants. WT, wild-­type unmodified CsUGT14 enzyme. Stbl; Stabilized 
variant of CsUGT14, Nd; not detected. (C) Glycosylation activity of the two most improved variants (B4, B15) from the second mutation round on variant S31 
background. The full enzyme assay is presented in SI Appendix, Fig. S15. (D–F) AlphaFold3-­based docking simulations showing structural differences between 
wild-­type CsUGT14 and the improved designs S31 and B4. In the wild-­type enzyme (D), bulky residues F151, Y204, and I89 sterically clash with THCA binding in 
a productive mode, and the hydroxyl and carboxyl moieties are too far from UDP-­Glc for effective glycosylation. In design S31 (E) substitutions F151M, Y204M, 
and I89M expand the active-­site pocket, enabling THCA positioning closer to UDP-­Glc. In design B4 (F), substitutions M89V, F125M, and M204I further enlarge 
the active site for better THCA accommodation.
